 2026 Midterm Elections Election Officials & Workers Trump threatened to interfere in the midterms. On Election Day, confrontation never came.
 Decisive margins left little room to challenge the results, but election officials still don’t know whether their preparations deterred the federal intervention they feared.
 By  Jessica Huseman  |  November 4, 2026, 11:03pm UTC 
 Republish lead-art-block.fullscreen-enter Expand A supporter of President Donald Trump wore a Trump 2028 shirt at the GOP election night watch party Tuesday in Bloomington, Minnesota. The Trump administration spent months threatening to intervene in the midterm elections, but Election Day passed calmly. (Jerry Holt / Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty) Get insider knowledge about how elections are run across the country. Sign up for Votebeat’s free weekly newsletter and never miss an update. 
 The Trump administration spent months threatening to intervene in the midterm elections, pursuing lawsuits against state election officials, investigating allegations of illegal voting , and repeatedly warning election workers they could face prosecution. 
 But when Election Day arrived on Tuesday, the extraordinary federal intervention that many election officials had spent months preparing for never came. By the end of the night, no major statewide or national Republican figure had disputed the results, and the process of certifying the election and preparing for a transfer of power appeared to be proceeding without major resistance. President Donald Trump himself told the New York Times he would accept the election results.
 Advocates and experts said they believe the months of preparations were key to avoiding a more dangerous outcome. That said, the relatively peaceful conclusion to an election marked by months of threats leaves election officials and voting rights advocates with little indication of how well their preparations would have held up against the federal intervention they feared, or what to expect in future elections.
 Margins too big to challenge
 One possible explanation for the abrupt change in tone became clearer as the results rolled in: Republicans lost too badly.
 “It’s a lot harder to steal a landslide defeat than a close outcome,” said Jonathan Diaz, who leads the Campaign Legal Center’s work defending election results and shoring up election administration.
 Even some of Trump’s most prominent allies acknowledge the importance of the margin.

 “When election results are not close …. no one looks under the hood,” Cleta Mitchell, a longtime Trump ally and conservative election activist, wrote Wednesday in a lengthy statement on X. “It is only when you have a very close election that people start examining the process.”
 Diaz sees close elections as openings for someone to try and overturn legitimate results. Mitchell appears to argue that close margins bring greater scrutiny of how elections are conducted. But their opposing views lead to the same conclusion: A decisive defeat leaves little room to challenge the outcome. Rather than dispute Tuesday’s results, Mitchell urged supporters to turn their attention to future fights over election laws.
 The administration’s efforts to influence the election were substantial, even without a dramatic Election Day confrontation. It pushed for unprecedented mid-decade redistricting , sought access to state voter information , filed lawsuits over alleged noncitizen voting and threatened election officials with prosecution. Courts blocked several of those efforts, including a last-minute attempt to force California officials to set aside thousands of ballots.
 Become a Votebeat sponsor “The courts pretty clearly rejected those efforts, but ultimately it was voters who put the final nail in the coffin on any large-scale election subversion by the administration,” Diaz said.
 Ben Hovland, a former chairman of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, also credited voters and election officials with limiting the administration’s ability to interfere. Trump fired Hovland in July , along with the commission’s other Democratic member, leaving the bipartisan federal agency responsible for voting system certification and election administration guidance without commissioners.
 “The administration’s efforts to undermine the midterm election results fizzled because Americans stood up for democracy,” said Hovland, now a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress. “In the end, the election officials’ prayer for high turnout and wide margins was answered and is likely a deterrence for further denial narratives post-election.”
 The preparations that weren’t tested
 Still, the decisive margins cannot fully explain why the administration didn’t take more extreme action before the results were known. Election officials spent months preparing for possible federal interference, but the absence of a confrontation makes it difficult to establish whether their preparations deterred any particular action.
 Jordan Barth, a voting rights advocate who previously worked on voter-protection operations for the Democratic National Committee and the 2024 Harris campaign, said he hopes the coordination developed this year becomes standard practice.
 State election officials and attorneys general developed contingency plans, emergency management groups prepared for disruptions, and campaigns worked with election officials to anticipate potential problems.
 “While thankfully the administration didn’t make good on their implicit and explicit threats over the last few months, I think that [much] of the coordination that was borne out of responding to these threats will continue,” Barth said.
 There are also contests still being decided. Melissa Michelson, a political science professor at Menlo College who studies voter behavior and turnout, said she was cautiously optimistic about the absence of extreme federal action but wasn’t prepared to rule out intervention in the weeks ahead, particularly in Alaska, where the Senate race remained close. 
 Pam Smith, president and CEO of Verified Voting, cautioned against treating the absence of federal intervention as permanent.
 “It’s a welcome pause from the worst threats, but a pause, not a resolution,” she said. “Election officials once could count on the federal government as a partner; at minimum they shouldn’t have to treat it as an adversary.”

 “Continuing to improve how we ensure safe and robust participation and well verified outcomes is what lets us withstand future challenges — even in close contests, not just when the margins are wide.”
 Jessica Huseman is Votebeat’s editorial director and is based in Dallas. Contact Jessica at jhuseman@votebeat.org .
